claims.source: These results demonstrate that the interaction of RNF68 with both FBXL10 and RNF2, which is necessary to form an active FRRUC, is also necessary for the assembly of DNA repair foci.
claims.evidence: Based on integration of mutant rescue experiments.

claims.claim: Disruption of the FRRUC negatively affects the recruitment of HRR factors to sites of DNA damage and the downstream DDR.
claims.source: Collectively, our results demonstrate that disruption of the FRRUC negatively affects the recruitment of HRR factors to sites of DNA damage and the downstream DDR.
claims.evidence: Based on integration of multiple DDR marker experiments.

claims.claim: DR-GFP cells depleted of FBXL10, RNF68, or RNF2 exhibit significantly diminished abilities to perform HRR.
claims.source: DR-GFP cells depleted of FBXL10, RNF68, or RNF2 exhibited significantly diminished abilities to perform HRR (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: Supported by DR-GFP reporter assay data shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: Mislocalization of the FRRUC by silencing PARP1 or TIMELESS results in reduced HRR capacity.
claims.source: Moreover, the mislocalization of the complex by silencing of PARP1 or TIMELESS also resulted in reduced HRR capacity (Figure 5E), in agreement with previous reports (Xie et al., 2015; Young et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by DR-GFP reporter assay data shown in Figure 5E and citations to Xie et al., 2015; Young et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Depletion of FBXL10, RNF68, RNF2, PARP1 or TIMELESS does not have any appreciable impact on cell cycle distribution.
claims.source: Importantly, depletion of FBXL10, RNF68, RNF2, PARP1 or TIMELESS did not have any appreciable impact on cell cycle distribution, as shown by BrdU-PI staining (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D), ensuring that the effects on the HHR pathway are not secondary to cell cycle differences.
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry cell cycle analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D.

claims.claim: No significant reduction in DNA repair mediated by NHEJ is observed upon depletion of RNF68 or RNF2.
claims.source: No significant reduction in DNA repair mediated by NHEJ was observed upon depletion of RNF68 or RNF2, as assessed by employing a cNHEJ assay based on the EJ5-GFP reporter U-2OS cell line (Bennardo et al., 2008) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E).
claims.evidence: Supported by EJ5-GFP reporter assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2E and citation to Bennardo et al., 2008.

claims.claim: Depletion of FBXL10 results in a reduction in NHEJ.
claims.source: Depletion of FBXL10 resulted in a reduction in NHEJ (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E), in agreement with the reduction in 53BP1 foci (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B–C), again, suggesting that FBXL10 may play a role in NHEJ independently of RNF68 and RNF2.
claims.evidence: Supported by EJ5-GFP reporter assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2E and 53BP1 foci data.

claims.claim: The reduction in the DDR and HRR in cells depleted of FBXL10, RNF68, or RNF2 correlates with an increased sensitivity to DNA damage.
claims.source: Finally, the reduction in the DDR and HRR in cells depleted of FBXL10, RNF68, or RNF2, correlated with an increased sensitivity to DNA damage as shown by the survival curves of cells treated with increasing concentrations of NCS (Figure 5—figure supplement 2F).
claims.evidence: Supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2F.

claims.claim: H2A levels are significantly reduced at FokI nuclease-induced DNA damage sites.
claims.source: We observed that, despite the relative increase in H2AK119Ub1 levels (Figure 3A–C), H2A levels were significantly reduced at the FokI nuclease-induced DNA damage sites (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), in agreement with previous reports (Batenburg et al., 2017; Berkovich et al., 2007; Strickfaden et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Supported by qChIP data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and citations to Batenburg et al., 2017; Berkovich et al., 2007; Strickfaden et al., 2016.

claims.claim: The reduction of H2A at DNA damage sites is inhibited by depletion of FBXL10, RNF68, or RNF2.
claims.source: Importantly, this reduction was inhibited by the depletion of FBXL10, RNF68, or RNF2, suggesting that the FRRUC is involved in the eviction of H2A near DNA damage sites (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Supported by qChIP data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: H2A.Z has been shown to be rapidly incorporated into sites of DNA damage and has been implicated in making the chromatin less compact to facilitate DNA repair.
claims.source: H2A.Z has been shown to be rapidly incorporated into sites of DNA damage and has been implicated in making the chromatin less compact to facilitate DNA repair (Alatwi and Downs, 2015; Gursoy-Yuzugullu et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Alatwi and Downs, 2015; Gursoy-Yuzugullu et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2012.

claims.claim: The ratio of H2A.Z over H2A is increased ~4.2 and ~10.2 kbp from DSBs 1 hour after FokI induction.
claims.source: To test whether the reduction in H2A is accompanied by a corresponding increase in the variant H2A.Z histone, we monitored the recruitment of H2A.Z to FokI-induced DSBs by qChIP 1 hr after induction, finding that the ratio of H2A.Z over H2A was increased ~4.2 and ~10.2 kbp from the DSB (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: Supported by qChIP data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: The increase in H2A.Z/H2A ratio at DSBs is abolished after depletion of FBXL10, RNF68, or RNF2.
claims.source: This increase was abolished after depletion of FBXL10, RNF68, or RNF2, demonstrating that the FRRUC is necessary for the enrichment of H2A.Z into sites of DNA damage (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: Supported by qChIP data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Four hours after induction of FokI, the relative enrichment of H2A.Z over H2A is still detectable, although to a lesser extent.
claims.source: Four hours after induction of FokI, the relative enrichment of H2A.Z over H2A was still detectable, although to a lesser extent (Figure 6B), in agreement with previous reports of transient incorporation of H2A.Z at DNA lesions (Gursoy-Yuzugullu et al., 2015; Kalocsay et al., 2009; Xu et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by qChIP data shown in Figure 6B and citations to Gursoy-Yuzugullu et al., 2015; Kalocsay et al., 2009; Xu et al., 2012.

claims.claim: H2A.Z is enriched at DNA damage sites as shown by dSTORM imaging.
claims.source: First, we confirmed that H2A.Z was enriched at DNA damage sites (Figure 6C), similarly to FBXL10, RNF68, and RNF2 (Figure 1A–B).
claims.evidence: Supported by dSTORM imaging data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: The magnitude of correlation between H2A.Z and γH2A.X diminishes upon depletion of FBXL10, RNF68, or RNF2.
claims.source: Importantly, analysis of H2A.Z and γH2A.X in cells treated with NCS showed that the magnitude of their correlation diminished upon depletion of FBXL10, RNF68, or RNF2 (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E), a further indication that the FRRUC is required for H2A.Z localization to sites of DNA damage.
claims.evidence: Supported by dSTORM cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: Mislocalization of the FRRUC through inhibition of PARP or depletion of PARP1 or TIMELESS results in failure to properly localize H2A.Z at sites of DNA damage.
claims.source: Accordingly, mislocalization of the FRRUC (through inhibition of PARP or depletion of PARP1 or TIMELESS) also resulted in the failure to properly localize H2A.Z at sites of DNA damage (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: Supported by dSTORM cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: Stable expression of siRNA-insensitive wild-type RNF68 rescues the effect of RNF68 depletion on H2A.Z recruitment.
claims.source: To control for possible off-target effects of the siRNA, we stably expressed an siRNA-insensitive RNF68 construct and found that it was able to rescue the effect of RNF68 depletion (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claims.claim: Stable expression of siRNA resistant RNF68(Y252D) or RNF68(ΔRING) is unable to complement the defect in H2A.Z recruitment in RNF68-depleted cells.
claims.source: In contrast, stable expression of either an siRNA resistant RNF68(Y252D) or an siRNA resistant RNF68(ΔRING) was unable to complement the defect in H2A.Z recruitment seen in RNF68-depleted cells (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1F), suggesting that the ability to bind both FBXL10 and RNF2 to establish an active FRRUC is important in this process.
claims.evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claims.claim: The FRRUC is required for proper H2A.Z recruitment to sites of DNA damage.
claims.source: Combined, these measurements establish that the FRRUC is required for proper H2A.Z recruitment to sites of DNA damage.
claims.evidence: Based on integration of multiple H2A.Z localization experiments.

claims.claim: In unperturbed human cells, the incorporation of H2A.Z-H2B dimers into nucleosomes relies on the SCRAP and P400 chromatin remodeler complexes.
claims.source: In unperturbed human cells, the incorporation of H2A.Z-H2B dimers into nucleosomes relies on the SCRAP and P400 chromatin remodeler complexes (Choi et al., 2009; Gévry et al., 2007; Ruhl et al., 2006), with the P400 complex being involved in the incorporation of H2A.Z also upon DSBs (Xu et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Choi et al., 2009; Gévry et al., 2007; Ruhl et al., 2006; Xu et al., 2012.

claims.claim: TIP48 and TIP49 accumulate on γH2A.X tracks after laser micro-irradiation.
claims.source: We used laser micro-irradiation to induce local DNA damage in human U-2OS cells, which was visualized by γH2A.X staining, and detected an accumulation of TIP48 and TIP49 on the γH2A.X tracks.
claims.evidence: Based on immunofluorescence microscopy observations.

claims.claim: Depletion of FBXL10, RNF68, or RNF2 does not affect the recruitment of TIP48 and TIP49 to DNA damage sites.
claims.source: We found that depletion of FBXL10, RNF68, or RNF2 did not affect the recruitment of TIP48 and TIP49 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G–H).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G-H.

claims.claim: Wild-type H2A and H2A(K119/120R) are equally incorporated in chromatin.
claims.source: These two constructs were equally incorporated in the chromatin, as detected by ChIP, and did not affect the amount of damage to the DNA, as detected by the levels of γH2A.X at the sites of damage (Figure 6—figure supplement 1I).
claims.evidence: Supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1I.

claims.claim: Overexpression of H2A(K119/120R) reduces H2A.Z loading at DSBs compared to control cells and cells overexpressing wild-type H2A.
claims.source: We observed a reduction in H2A.Z loading at DSBs in cells overexpressing H2A(K119/120R) compared to control cells and cells overexpressing wild-type H2A (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: Supported by qChIP data shown in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: The FRRUC-dependent mono-ubiquitylation of H2A is required for proper H2A.Z loading.
claims.source: This result is in agreement with the fact that only wild-type RNF68, but not the two inactive RNF68 mutants, rescued the defect of H2A.Z loading (Figure 6E), and indicates that the FRRUC-dependent mono-ubiquitylation of H2A is required for proper H2A.Z loading.
claims.evidence: Based on integration of H2A mutant and RNF68 mutant rescue experiments.

claims.claim: H2A mono-ubiquitylation is not impaired upon H2A.Z silencing.
claims.source: While H2A mono-ubiquitylation was not impaired upon H2A.Z silencing (Figure 7A), we detected significantly more nascent RNA transcript production near DSB sites in H2A.Z depleted cells compared control cells (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: Significantly more nascent RNA transcript production occurs near DSB sites in H2A.Z depleted cells compared to control cells.
claims.source: While H2A mono-ubiquitylation was not impaired upon H2A.Z silencing (Figure 7A), we detected significantly more nascent RNA transcript production near DSB sites in H2A.Z depleted cells compared control cells (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: Supported by YFP-MS2 reporter assay data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: H2A.Z silencing does not have a negative effect on FokI nuclease levels.
claims.source: [H2A.Z silencing did not have a negative effect on FokI nuclease levels (Figure 7—figure supplement 1)].
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: There is a decrease in both 5-EU incorporation and phosphorylation of RNAPII on Ser2 at laser induced damage sites in control cells, and this decrease is significantly less in H2A.Z depleted cells.
claims.source: Similarly, there was a decrease in both 5-EU incorporation and phosphorylation of RNAPII on Ser2 at laser induced damage sites in control cells, and this decrease was significantly less in cells in which H2A.Z was depleted (Figure 7C–D).
claims.evidence: Supported by 5-EU incorporation and RNAPII Ser2 immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7C-D.

claims.claim: H2A.Z depletion induces a reduction in the phosphorylation of RPA2 on Ser4, Ser8, and Ser33 as well as in the phosphorylation of CHK1 (Ser317).
claims.source: Similar to the depletion of the FRRUC, H2A.Z depletion in both U-2OS and MIA-PaCa-2 cells also induced a reduction in the phosphorylation of RPA2 on Ser4, Ser8, and Ser33 as well as in the phosphorylation of CHK1 (Ser317) (Figure 7E), all events necessary for efficient HRR repair.
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: No changes in γH2A.X levels are observed upon H2A.Z silencing.
claims.source: Again, we observed no changes in γH2A.X levels upon H2A.Z silencing, showing that the amount of DNA damage induction was similar in all conditions (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: H2A.Z is required for efficient HRR.
claims.source: Finally, we found that H2A.Z is required for efficient HRR (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: Supported by DR-GFP reporter assay data shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: H2A.Z incorporation contributes to transcriptional silencing after DNA damage, as well as efficient DNA damage signaling and HRR.
claims.source: Altogether, these results indicate that H2A.Z incorporation, which is downstream to the FRRUC and H2AK119Ub1, contributes to transcriptional silencing after DNA damage, as well as efficient DNA damage signaling and HRR.
claims.evidence: Based on integration of multiple H2A.Z depletion experiments.

claims.claim: The FRRUC is recruited to sites of DNA damage in a PARP1- and TIMELESS-dependent manner.
claims.source: We show here that the FRRUC is recruited to sites of DNA damage in a PARP1- and TIMELESS-dependent manner.
claims.evidence: Based on integration of recruitment experiments with PARP1 and TIMELESS depletion/inhibition.

claims.claim: The FRRUC is required for efficient mono-ubiquitylation of histone H2A on K119 at DNA damage sites.
claims.source: Our results demonstrate that the complex is required for efficient mono-ubiquitylation of histone H2A on K119, a decrease of H2A levels at DSBs, localization of the histone variant H2A.Z to sites of DNA damage, transcriptional repression, DSB signaling, and proper HRR (see model in Figure 7F).
claims.evidence: Based on integration of multiple experimental results.

claims.claim: The FRRUC promotes a decrease of H2A levels at DSBs.
claims.source: Our results demonstrate that the complex is required for efficient mono-ubiquitylation of histone H2A on K119, a decrease of H2A levels at DSBs, localization of the histone variant H2A.Z to sites of DNA damage, transcriptional repression, DSB signaling, and proper HRR (see model in Figure 7F).
claims.evidence: Based on qChIP data showing H2A reduction is FRRUC-dependent.

claims.claim: The FRRUC promotes localization of H2A.Z to sites of DNA damage.
claims.source: Our results demonstrate that the complex is required for efficient mono-ubiquitylation of histone H2A on K119, a decrease of H2A levels at DSBs, localization of the histone variant H2A.Z to sites of DNA damage, transcriptional repression, DSB signaling, and proper HRR (see model in Figure 7F).
claims.evidence: Based on qChIP and dSTORM data showing H2A.Z recruitment is FRRUC-dependent.

claims.claim: The FRRUC promotes transcriptional repression at DNA damage sites.
claims.source: Our results demonstrate that the complex is required for efficient mono-ubiquitylation of histone H2A on K119, a decrease of H2A levels at DSBs, localization of the histone variant H2A.Z to sites of DNA damage, transcriptional repression, DSB signaling, and proper HRR (see model in Figure 7F).
claims.evidence: Based on multiple transcription reporter assays.

claims.claim: The FRRUC promotes DSB signaling.
claims.source: Our results demonstrate that the complex is required for efficient mono-ubiquitylation of histone H2A on K119, a decrease of H2A levels at DSBs, localization of the histone variant H2A.Z to sites of DNA damage, transcriptional repression, DSB signaling, and proper HRR (see model in Figure 7F).
claims.evidence: Based on DDR marker experiments showing reduced signaling upon FRRUC depletion.

claims.claim: The FRRUC promotes proper HRR.
claims.source: Our results demonstrate that the complex is required for efficient mono-ubiquitylation of histone H2A on K119, a decrease of H2A levels at DSBs, localization of the histone variant H2A.Z to sites of DNA damage, transcriptional repression, DSB signaling, and proper HRR (see model in Figure 7F).
claims.evidence: Based on DR-GFP reporter assay data.

claims.claim: Transcriptional silencing in response to genotoxic stress facilitates DNA damage resolution by ensuring that the transcriptional machinery does not interfere sterically with DNA damage repair factors.
claims.source: In response to genotoxic stress, transcriptional silencing is thought to facilitate DNA damage resolution by ensuring that the transcriptional machinery does not interfere sterically with DNA damage repair factors (e.g. by avoiding the collision of the elongating RNA Polymerase complex with DNA repair complexes) (Uckelmann and Sixma, 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Uckelmann and Sixma, 2017.

claims.claim: Several factors and complexes have been implicated in DNA damage-induced transcriptional repression.
claims.source: Several factors and complexes, such as NurRD, PBAF, ENL, RNF8, NELF-E, and RNF51-UBR5 have been implicated in the DNA damage-induced transcriptional repression (Awwad et al., 2017; Chou et al., 2010; Gong et al., 2017; Kakarougkas et al., 2014; Paul and Wang, 2017; Sanchez et al., 2016, 2010; Ui et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claims.claim: The mono-ubiquitylation of histone H2A on K119 is largely impaired by the depletion of the FRRUC.
claims.source: We found that the mono-ubiquitylation of histone H2A on K119 is largely impaired by the depletion of the FRRUC.
claims.evidence: Based on immunofluorescence and qChIP data.

claims.claim: The FRRUC is a major contributor to the mono-ubiquitylation of histone H2A on K119 in transcriptional regulation.
claims.source: Similarly, the FRRUC is a major contributor to the mono-ubiquitylation of histone H2A on K119 in transcriptional regulation (Blackledge et al., 2014; Rose et al., 2016; Taherbhoy et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Blackledge et al., 2014; Rose et al., 2016; Taherbhoy et al., 2015.

claims.claim: The FRRUC is necessary for the proper recruitment of RNF51-RNF2 and RNF110-RNF2 in response to genotoxic stress.
claims.source: Our results show that the FRRUC is necessary for the proper recruitment of these two cPRC1s in response to genotoxic stress.
claims.evidence: Based on live cell imaging recruitment experiments.

claims.claim: The FRRUC is the most upstream ubiquitin ligase in charge of mono-ubiquitylating histone H2A on K119 at DNA damage sites.
claims.source: Moreover, our findings suggest that the FRRUC is the most upstream ubiquitin ligase in charge of mono-ubiquitylating histone H2A on K119 and that, subsequently, cPRC1s maintain this modification.
claims.evidence: Based on integration of recruitment kinetics and dependency experiments.

claims.claim: Compared to the recruitment of 70 DNA repair proteins measured in a recent study, FBXL10, RNF68, and RNF2 display very fast recruitment.
claims.source: Interestingly, a recent study measured the kinetics of recruitment of 70 DNA repair proteins to laser-induced DNA damage sites in HeLa cells (Aleksandrov et al., 2018). Compared to the recruitment of these 70 proteins, FBXL10, RNF68, and RNF2 display a very fast recruitment, suggesting that this represent one of the most upstream events in response to genotoxic stress.
claims.evidence: Based on comparison to published kinetics data from Aleksandrov et al., 2018.

claims.claim: The DNA damage response frequently re-purposes the function of specific transcriptional regulators to enact DNA repair.
claims.source: The DNA damage response frequently re-purposes the function of specific transcriptional regulators to enact DNA repair (Sarcinella et al., 2007; Shiloh and Ziv, 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Sarcinella et al., 2007; Shiloh and Ziv, 2013.

claims.claim: The presence, localization, and activity of the FRRUC is required for an efficient H2A/H2A.Z exchange at DNA lesions.
claims.source: Our results reveal that the presence, localization, and activity of the FRRUC, in addition to mono-ubiquitylate H2A on K119 (as in unstressed cells), is also required for an efficient H2A/H2A.Z exchange at DNA lesions.
claims.evidence: Based on integration of H2A and H2A.Z qChIP and imaging data.

claims.claim: H2A.Z is not required for H2A mono-ubiquitylation.
claims.source: Notably, whereas H2A.Z is not required for H2A mono-ubiquitylation, the FRRUC-dependent mono-ubiquitylation of H2A is required for proper H2A.Z loading.
claims.evidence: Based on H2A.Z depletion experiments showing no effect on H2AK119Ub1.

claims.claim: The FRRUC-dependent mono-ubiquitylation of H2A is required for proper H2A.Z loading.
claims.source: Notably, whereas H2A.Z is not required for H2A mono-ubiquitylation, the FRRUC-dependent mono-ubiquitylation of H2A is required for proper H2A.Z loading.
claims.evidence: Based on H2A mutant and FRRUC depletion experiments.

claims.claim: H2A.Z has been shown to function in the early stages of DNA repair.
claims.source: H2A.Z has been shown to function in the early stages of DNA repair (Adkins et al., 2013; Alatwi and Downs, 2015; Gursoy-Yuzugullu et al., 2015; Jiang et al., 2015; Kalocsay et al., 2009; Xu et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claims.claim: H2A.Z is rapidly, yet transiently, recruited to DSBs.
claims.source: H2A.Z is rapidly, yet transiently, recruited to DSBs (Alatwi and Downs, 2015; Gursoy-Yuzugullu et al., 2015; Kalocsay et al., 2009; Kusch et al., 2004; Nishibuchi et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claims.claim: H2A.Z shares 56% sequence identity with H2A.
claims.source: H2A.Z shares 56% sequence identity with H2A and the differences account for a structurally less stable interface between H2A.Z and the H3-H4 subunits of the nucleosome.
claims.evidence: Based on established knowledge of histone variant sequences.

claims.claim: H2A.Z makes weakened, loose nucleosomes that are easy to bend and disassemble, leading to a more accessible chromatin.
claims.source: In fact, H2A.Z appears to make weakened, loose nucleosomes that are easy to bend and disassemble, leading to a more accessible chromatin (Bönisch et al., 2012; Jin and Felsenfeld, 2007; Jin et al., 2009; Suto et al., 2000; Xu et al., 2012), which may favor recruitment of DNA repair factors.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Bönisch et al., 2012; Jin and Felsenfeld, 2007; Jin et al., 2009; Suto et al., 2000; Xu et al., 2012.

claims.claim: H2A.Z has been associated with both positive and negative transcriptional regulation depending on its post-translational modifications.
claims.source: H2A.Z has been associated with both positive and negative transcriptional regulation depending on its post-translational modifications (Guillemette and Gaudreau, 2006; Hu et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Guillemette and Gaudreau, 2006; Hu et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Mono-ubiquitylation of H2A.Z on K120 and K121 is correlated with transcriptional silencing.
claims.source: Mono-ubiquitylation of H2A.Z on K120 and K121 is correlated with transcriptional silencing (Draker et al., 2011; Sarcinella et al., 2007), whereas H2A.Z acetylation on its N-terminus is associated with transcriptional activity (Valdés-Mora et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Draker et al., 2011; Sarcinella et al., 2007.

claims.claim: H2A.Z acetylation on its N-terminus is associated with transcriptional activity.
claims.source: Mono-ubiquitylation of H2A.Z on K120 and K121 is correlated with transcriptional silencing (Draker et al., 2011; Sarcinella et al., 2007), whereas H2A.Z acetylation on its N-terminus is associated with transcriptional activity (Valdés-Mora et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Valdés-Mora et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Mono-ubiquitylation of H2A.Z has been attributed to RNF2 activity.
claims.source: Interestingly, mono-ubiquitylation of H2A.Z has been attributed to RNF2 activity (Sarcinella et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Sarcinella et al., 2007.

claims.claim: The FRRUC could be involved in transcriptional silencing by mono-ubiquitylating H2A, facilitating exchange of H2A with H2A.Z, and mono-ubiquitylating H2A.Z.
claims.source: Thus, the FRRUC could be involved in transcriptional silencing by several non-exclusive – and, perhaps, linked – means: (i) mono-ubiquitylating H2A, (ii) facilitating exchange of a subpopulation of H2A with H2A.Z, and (iii), mono-ubiquitylating H2A.Z.
claims.evidence: Based on integration of experimental results and speculation about mechanisms.

claims.claim: Upon DNA damage, H2A.Z can simultaneously 'loosen' the chromatin to facilitate access to DNA repair factors and mediate transcriptional silencing.
claims.source: It is possible that, upon DNA damage, H2A.Z can simultaneously 'loosen' the chromatin to facilitate the access to DNA repair factors (this is the reason for which a subpopulation of H2A is exchanged for H2A.Z) and mediate transcriptional silencing (conceivably, by its mono-ubiquitylation).
claims.evidence: Speculative interpretation of experimental results.

claims.claim: PARP1 has been implicated in H2A displacement and chromatin decondensation after DNA damage.
claims.source: Accordingly, PARP1 has been implicated in H2A displacement and chromatin decondensation after DNA damage (Sellou et al., 2016; Strickfaden et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Sellou et al., 2016; Strickfaden et al., 2016.

claims.claim: The regulation of FBXL10, RNF68, and RNF2 by TIMELESS is unusual since the recruitment of other PARP-dependent factors is not affected by TIMELESS depletion.
claims.source: The regulation of FBXL10, RNF68, and RNF2 by TIMELESS is unusual since the recruitment of other factors downstream of PARP, such as XRCC1 and Ligase 3 (that are required for single strand break and base excision repair), is affected by PARP1 silencing (Campalans et al., 2013; Godon et al., 2008; Mortusewicz et al., 2006; Okano et al., 2003), but not by TIMELESS depletion, suggesting a specific role of TIMELESS in controlling DSB repair.
claims.evidence: Based on comparison of TIMELESS effects on different DNA repair factors and citations.

claims.claim: In response to DNA damage, H2A and H2A.X are ubiquitylated on both K13 and K15 in addition to mono-ubiquitylation of K119/K120.
claims.source: In response to DNA damage, in addition to the mono-ubiquitylation of K119/K120, H2A and H2A.X are also ubiquitylated on both K13 and K15.
claims.evidence: Based on established knowledge of histone ubiquitylation in DDR.

claims.claim: RNF8 decorates H1 type linker histones and L3MBTL2 with K63-linked ubiquitin chains in response to DNA damage.
claims.source: This event requires two steps: first, an RNF ubiquitin ligase, namely RNF8, decorates H1 type linker histones and L3MBTL2 with K63-linked ubiquitin chains (Mandemaker et al., 2017; Nowsheen et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Mandemaker et al., 2017; Nowsheen et al., 2018.

claims.claim: RNF168 recognizes K63-linked ubiquitin chains on H1 and L3MBTL2 and mono-ubiquitylates H2A and H2A.X on K13 and K15.
claims.source: Next, these chains are recognized by RNF168, another RNF ubiquitin ligase, that mono-ubiquitylates H2A and H2A.X on K13 and K15 (Gatti et al., 2012; Leung et al., 2014; Mattiroli et al., 2012; Thorslund et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Gatti et al., 2012; Leung et al., 2014; Mattiroli et al., 2012; Thorslund et al., 2015.

claims.claim: A K63 chain is built on mono-ubiquitylated H2A and H2A.X, although the ubiquitin ligase involved in this elongation step is still debated.
claims.source: Ultimately, a K63 chain (and, possibly other kind of ubiquitin chains) is/are built on mono-ubiquitylated H2A and H2A.X, although the ubiquitin ligase involved in this elongation step is still debated (Uckelmann and Sixma, 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Uckelmann and Sixma, 2017.

results.result: The FRRUC (FBXL10-RNF68-RNF2 complex) is recruited to DNA damage sites. The three proteins form a trimeric complex (C1), endogenous proteins co-localize with γH2A.X at damage sites (C2), and super-resolution imaging shows significant enrichment at DNA damage sites upon NCS treatment (C3).
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 provide converging evidence from co-immunoprecipitation (C1), immunofluorescence microscopy (C2), and dSTORM super-resolution imaging with cross-correlation analysis (C3). The multiple orthogonal techniques strengthen the conclusion that the FRRUC is recruited to DNA damage sites.

results.result: The FRRUC is rapidly recruited to laser-induced DNA damage sites with peak recruitment within one minute. GFP-FBXL10, mCherry-RNF68, and GFP-RNF2 are recruited within seconds (C6), peak recruitment occurs within one minute (C7), and RNF2 remains at lesions longer than FBXL10 and RNF68 (C8).
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C8 are supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 1C with quantitative kinetics measurements. The temporal resolution and quantification provide strong evidence for the rapid recruitment kinetics. The differential persistence of RNF2 is consistent with its participation in multiple complexes.

results.result: PARP1 and TIMELESS are required for FRRUC recruitment to DNA damage sites. PARP inhibition with Olaparib completely abolishes recruitment (C10, C12), while ATM, ATR, or DNA-PK inhibition does not (C11), and depletion of either PARP1 or TIMELESS abolishes recruitment (C16).
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C12 and C16 are supported by live cell imaging data with pharmacological inhibitors and siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 1C and supplementary figures. The specificity for PARP1/TIMELESS versus other DNA damage kinases strengthens the conclusion. Controls for knockdown efficiency are provided.

results.result: The FRRUC is required for proper recruitment of cPRC1 complexes (RNF51-RNF2 and RNF110-RNF2) to DNA damage sites. FBXL10 and RNF68 recruitment is independent of RNF51/RNF110 (C21), but RNF51 and RNF110 recruitment depends on PARP1, TIMELESS, and an active FRRUC (C24, C29, C30).
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C31 are supported by live cell imaging recruitment experiments with siRNA knockdown and rescue experiments using RNF68 mutants (Figure 2). The epistasis analysis showing FRRUC acts upstream of cPRC1s is well-supported. The rescue experiments with structure-function mutants (Y252D and ΔRING) provide strong mechanistic evidence.

results.result: Specific amino acids in RNF68 mediate interactions with FBXL10 and RNF2. Four amino acids (QYSV at positions 251-254) are essential for FBXL10 binding (C25), Y252D mutation disrupts FBXL10 binding without affecting RNF2 interaction (C26), Y252A has no effect (C27), and RING domain deletion abrogates RNF2 binding while preserving FBXL10 interaction (C28).
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C28 are supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments with truncation and point mutants shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2. The structure-function analysis is systematic and provides clear separation-of-function mutants. These mutants are subsequently used in functional rescue experiments, strengthening their validity.

results.result: The FRRUC mediates H2AK119Ub1 at DNA damage sites. Knockdown of FBXL10, RNF68, or RNF2 reduces H2AK119Ub1 staining on laser damage tracks (C32), as does PARP1/TIMELESS silencing (C33). Rescue experiments confirm specificity (C34), and qChIP shows H2AK119Ub1 induction ~4.2 and ~10.2 kbp from DSBs that is FRRUC-dependent (C35, C36).
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C36 are supported by immunofluorescence quantification (Figure 3A) and qChIP experiments (Figure 3C) using the FokI reporter system. The rescue experiments with RNF68 mutants (C34) control for off-target effects. The spatial resolution of qChIP provides quantitative evidence for H2AK119Ub1 spreading from DSBs.

results.result: The FRRUC is required for transcriptional silencing at DNA damage sites. Nascent RNA production is abolished in control cells upon FokI activation (C38), but significantly restored upon FRRUC depletion or mislocalization (C40, C42). RNAPII Ser2 phosphorylation shows similar patterns (C43). ATM inhibition also restores transcription (C39).
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C44 are supported by multiple orthogonal transcription assays: YFP-MS2 reporter (Figure 4B), 5-EU incorporation (Figure 4D), and RNAPII Ser2 phosphorylation (Figure 4E). The convergence of multiple readouts strengthens the conclusion. Controls for FokI nuclease levels are provided (C41).

results.result: The FRRUC promotes DNA damage signaling and recruitment of HRR factors. FRRUC depletion reduces RAD51, BRCA1, and pRPA2 foci (C45, C47, C48) without affecting total RAD51 levels (C46) or γH2A.X/MDC1 foci (C51, C53). Phosphorylation of RPA2 and CHK1 is reduced (C49, C50), as are ubiquitin-positive foci (C52). Rescue experiments with RNF68 mutants confirm specificity (C54, C55).
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C57 are supported by extensive immunofluorescence foci counting (Figure 5A-B and supplements) and immunoblotting (Figure 5D). The rescue experiments with structure-function mutants (C54, C55) control for off-target effects. The preservation of γH2A.X levels (C51) indicates similar DNA damage induction across conditions. The epistasis analysis places FRRUC downstream of MDC1 but upstream of RPA2 phosphorylation and RAD51 recruitment.

results.result: The FRRUC is required for efficient homologous recombination repair (HRR). DR-GFP cells depleted of FBXL10, RNF68, or RNF2 show significantly diminished HRR (C58), as do cells with mislocalized FRRUC due to PARP1 or TIMELESS silencing (C59). Cell cycle distribution is unaffected by these depletions (C60).
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C60 are supported by DR-GFP reporter assay data (Figure 5E) and flow cytometry cell cycle analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D). The cell cycle control (C60) is critical as it rules out indirect effects through altered cell cycle distribution. The consistency with prior reports on PARP1/TIMELESS (C59) strengthens confidence.

results.result: The FRRUC shows pathway specificity for HRR versus NHEJ. No significant reduction in NHEJ is observed upon RNF68 or RNF2 depletion (C61), but FBXL10 depletion reduces NHEJ (C62), suggesting FBXL10 may have NHEJ functions independent of RNF68 and RNF2.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C62 are supported by EJ5-GFP reporter assay data (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E). The differential effects of FBXL10 versus RNF68/RNF2 depletion on NHEJ are consistent with FBXL10's participation in other protein complexes. The 53BP1 foci data support the NHEJ phenotype for FBXL10.

results.result: H2A levels are reduced at DNA damage sites in a FRRUC-dependent manner. H2A levels are significantly reduced at FokI-induced DSBs (C64), and this reduction is inhibited by FBXL10, RNF68, or RNF2 depletion (C65), suggesting the FRRUC is involved in H2A eviction.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C65 are supported by qChIP data (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) and are consistent with prior reports. The FRRUC-dependence of H2A reduction suggests a mechanistic link between H2AK119Ub1 and histone eviction. However, the mechanism by which ubiquitylation leads to eviction is not directly demonstrated.

results.result: The FRRUC is required for H2A.Z recruitment to DNA damage sites. The H2A.Z/H2A ratio increases at DSBs 1 hour after FokI induction (C67), and this increase is abolished by FRRUC depletion (C68). The enrichment is transient (C69) and confirmed by dSTORM imaging (C70, C71). Mislocalization of FRRUC also impairs H2A.Z recruitment (C72). Rescue experiments with RNF68 mutants confirm specificity (C73, C74).
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C75 are supported by qChIP data (Figure 6A-B) and dSTORM cross-correlation analysis (Figure 6C-D). The use of orthogonal techniques (qChIP and super-resolution imaging) strengthens the conclusion. The rescue experiments with structure-function mutants (C73, C74) control for off-target effects. The temporal dynamics (C69) are consistent with prior reports.

results.result: TIP48 and TIP49 recruitment to DNA damage sites is independent of the FRRUC. Depletion of FBXL10, RNF68, or RNF2 does not affect TIP48 and TIP49 recruitment (C78).
results.evaluation: Claim C78 is supported by immunofluorescence data (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G-H). This negative result is important as it suggests the FRRUC does not regulate H2A.Z incorporation through TIP48/TIP49 recruitment, but rather through a different mechanism, possibly involving H2A ubiquitylation.

results.result: FRRUC-dependent H2A mono-ubiquitylation is required for H2A.Z loading. Wild-type H2A and H2A(K119/120R) are equally incorporated in chromatin (C79), but overexpression of H2A(K119/120R) reduces H2A.Z loading at DSBs (C80), indicating that H2A mono-ubiquitylation is required for proper H2A.Z loading (C81).
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C81 are supported by qChIP data (Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1I). The H2A(K119/120R) mutant provides a direct test of the requirement for H2A ubiquitylation in H2A.Z loading. The control showing equal chromatin incorporation (C79) is important. This result is consistent with the RNF68 mutant rescue experiments.

results.result: H2A.Z contributes to transcriptional silencing, DNA damage signaling, and HRR downstream of the FRRUC. H2A mono-ubiquitylation is not impaired by H2A.Z silencing (C82), but H2A.Z depletion increases nascent RNA production near DSBs (C83), reduces 5-EU incorporation and RNAPII Ser2 phosphorylation at damage sites (C85), reduces RPA2 and CHK1 phosphorylation (C86), and impairs HRR (C88). γH2A.X levels are unaffected (C87).
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C89 are supported by multiple assays: immunofluorescence (Figure 7A), YFP-MS2 reporter (Figure 7B), 5-EU incorporation and RNAPII Ser2 staining (Figure 7C-D), immunoblotting (Figure 7E), and DR-GFP reporter (Figure 5E). The epistasis analysis showing H2A.Z acts downstream of H2AK119Ub1 (C82) is important. The convergence of multiple readouts strengthens the conclusion that H2A.Z contributes to multiple aspects of the DDR.

results.result: The FRRUC is recruited to DNA damage sites in a PARP1- and TIMELESS-dependent manner and promotes H2AK119Ub1, H2A eviction, H2A.Z localization, transcriptional repression, DSB signaling, and HRR. This represents an integration of the major findings of the manuscript.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C96 represent the main conclusions of the manuscript, integrating results from multiple experimental approaches. Each component is supported by the specific results evaluated above. The model in Figure 7F summarizes these findings. The pathway from PARP1/TIMELESS → FRRUC → H2AK119Ub1 → H2A.Z incorporation → transcriptional silencing and HRR is well-supported by the data.

results.result: The FRRUC is the most upstream ubiquitin ligase responsible for H2AK119Ub1 at DNA damage sites, with cPRC1s maintaining this modification. This is inferred from recruitment kinetics and dependency experiments showing FRRUC recruits before cPRC1s and is required for cPRC1 recruitment.
results.evaluation: Claim C102 is supported by the integration of recruitment kinetics data (Figure 1C, Figure 2B-C) and epistasis experiments (Figure 2A). The rapid recruitment of FRRUC (peak ~1 min) compared to cPRC1s (peak ~75 s) and the requirement of FRRUC for cPRC1 recruitment support this conclusion. However, the claim that cPRC1s 'maintain' the modification is more speculative and not directly tested.

results.result: FBXL10, RNF68, and RNF2 display very fast recruitment compared to 70 other DNA repair proteins measured in a recent study, suggesting this represents one of the most upstream events in response to genotoxic stress.
results.evaluation: Claim C103 is supported by comparison to published kinetics data from Aleksandrov et al., 2018. The peak recruitment within ~1 minute is indeed very rapid. However, the claim relies on a comparison to a different study in different cells (HeLa vs U-2OS), which introduces some uncertainty. The conclusion is reasonable but should be interpreted with caution.

results.result: The FRRUC-dependent mono-ubiquitylation of H2A is required for H2A.Z loading, but H2A.Z is not required for H2A mono-ubiquitylation. This establishes the epistatic relationship between H2AK119Ub1 and H2A.Z incorporation.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C107 are supported by the integration of H2A.Z depletion experiments (Figure 7A showing no effect on H2AK119Ub1) and H2A(K119/120R) overexpression experiments (Figure 6F showing reduced H2A.Z loading). This epistasis analysis clearly places H2AK119Ub1 upstream of H2A.Z incorporation. The mechanism by which ubiquitylation promotes H2A.Z loading is not elucidated but is discussed speculatively.

results.result: The FRRUC could be involved in transcriptional silencing by multiple means: mono-ubiquitylating H2A, facilitating H2A/H2A.Z exchange, and mono-ubiquitylating H2A.Z. H2A.Z may simultaneously loosen chromatin to facilitate DNA repair factor access and mediate transcriptional silencing.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C117 are explicitly speculative (marked as SPECULATION in evidence_type). While the data support that the FRRUC mono-ubiquitylates H2A and promotes H2A.Z incorporation, and that both contribute to transcriptional silencing, the specific mechanisms and whether H2A.Z is mono-ubiquitylated by the FRRUC at DNA damage sites are not directly tested. These are reasonable hypotheses for future work but not demonstrated results.

results.result: The regulation of FBXL10, RNF68, and RNF2 by TIMELESS is unusual since other PARP-dependent factors (XRCC1, Ligase 3) are not affected by TIMELESS depletion, suggesting a specific role of TIMELESS in controlling DSB repair.
results.evaluation: Claim C119 is supported by the differential effects of TIMELESS depletion on FRRUC recruitment (abolished, Figure 1C) versus XRCC1/Ligase 3 recruitment (unaffected, Figure 1—figure supplement 3B). This specificity is notable and suggests TIMELESS has distinct roles in different DNA repair pathways. The interpretation is reasonable given the data.

results.result: ATM inhibition increases FRRUC recruitment, and ATM might limit the spread of the FRRUC and H2A mono-ubiquitylation to maintain the signal at DSB proximities.
results.evaluation: Claim C128 is supported by observed recruitment kinetics with ATM inhibitor (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D). However, claim C129 is explicitly speculative. While the observation of increased recruitment with ATM inhibition is interesting, the interpretation that ATM limits FRRUC spread is not directly tested. Spatial analysis of FRRUC distribution with and without ATM inhibition would be needed to support this claim.

results.result: The recruitment of the FRRUC represents an early and critical regulatory step in HRR. This is the main conclusion of the manuscript.
results.evaluation: Claim C130 is supported by the integration of all experimental results showing: (1) early recruitment kinetics (within 1 minute), (2) requirement for multiple downstream events (H2AK119Ub1, H2A.Z incorporation, transcriptional silencing, RAD51 recruitment), and (3) functional requirement for HRR (DR-GFP assay). The evidence strongly supports that FRRUC recruitment is an early and critical step in HRR.
